newsitem.title: FRANCE: France sees good response to Zaire force plan.
newsitem.headline: France sees good response to Zaire force plan.

text.p: France said on Tuesday it was getting a favourable response to its proposal to send a multinational force to ensure security for more than a million starving refugees in eastern Zaire.
But formidable diplomatic obstacles remained as the clock ticked away for the refugees, deprived of food by fighting between Zairean troops and Rwanda-backed Tutsi rebels.
French President Jacques Chirac said the proposed force was crucial to help ensure that aid got through to the refugees, whose plight he called tragic.

He said the force, comprising soldiers "from all major nations, particularly the United States", must first be approved by the United Nations Security Council, after which Africans should rapidly take over.

"We have suggested sending a force to ensure security... which should be decided upon by the Security Council and could as soon as possible be replaced by an African force with U.S. and European backing," Chirac told a news conference.
He said Paris had started consultations with Washington and the Security Council would hold an emergency meeting later in the day.
French foreign ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said European Union experts on Africa were meeting in Brussels and would consult later in the day with American, Canadian and African diplomats.

France, still smarting from charges that it furthered its own interests by intervening in Zaire and Rwanda in 1994 in the aftermath of a Hutu massacre of Tutsis, has made clear it needs international backing.
"France does not want to act alone," Rummelhardt said.
Rwanda's Tutsi-dominated government warned on Tuesday that it would oppose international intervention in eastern Zaire "by all means, not only political".
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said Washington, which has requested clarification of the proposal, was interested in the French initiative.
So far only Spain, whose prime minister Jose Maria Aznar was meeting Chirac for a bilateral summit in Marseille, has agreed to participate in the proposed force.
British ministers have made clear they will not be rushed into a poorly thought-out operation in a part of Africa where Britain has hardly any interests.
An Italian foreign ministry spokesman said there was no question at this stage of committing any European troops.

Leaders of east and central African states gathered in Nairobi to discuss the situation in eastern Zaire but hopes for progress dimmed as Kenya said Zairean Prime Minister Kengo Wa Dondo would not attend.

Chirac insisted that ailing Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko, who has been out of his his country undergoing medical treatment for more than three months, had a crucial role to play in solving the conflict.

"It is quite obvious that the international community cannot ignore that he is the man best placed to represent Zaire and find a solution to this problem as far as Zaire is concerned," the French leader said.
Mobutu, 66, remained secluded at his French Riviera villa near Nice and was due to meet U.N. representative Raymond Chretien on Wednesday.
He arrived unexpectedly on Monday from Switzerland where he was being treated for prostate cancer. He is expected to fly to Zaire in a few days.
